To ingest something means to take it into the body — most often through the mouth, by swallowing. It is the formal, precise word for what happens when you eat food, drink water, take a pill, or accidentally swallow something you didn't mean to.

A simple way to picture it: imagine the body as a container with an opening at the top (the mouth). To ingest something is to move it from the outside world into that container, where the body will then deal with it.

The one doing the ingesting is always a living organism. A person ingests medicine. An animal ingests its prey. Even a single cell in biology can ingest bacteria — the cell literally surrounds and absorbs the bacteria — and scientists use the word "ingest" to describe this too.

Almost any substance that enters the body through the mouth can be described as ingested: food, water, medicine, alcohol, poison, a foreign object (like when a child accidentally swallows a small toy), and even gases or fumes in certain scientific contexts. The word is not limited to food — this is exactly what makes it both powerful and precise.

These words are close relatives, but they are not the same.

"Eat" is casual and specific to food. You eat a sandwich. You wouldn't normally say you "eat" a pill or "eat" poison.

"Drink" is specific to liquids.

"Swallow" describes the physical, mechanical action of moving something down your throat. It focuses on how something goes in, not what happens after.

"Ingest" is broader than all of these. It covers any substance — food, liquid, medication, poison, or an object — taken into the body. And unlike "swallow," it doesn't focus on the physical motion but on the outcome: the substance is now inside the body's system. This is precisely why doctors, scientists, and toxicologists prefer "ingest" — it is accurate regardless of what the substance is.

"Ingest" is a formal and clinical word. You won't hear it much in everyday conversation — nobody says "I just ingested a burger." You will find it in medical writing ("Do not ingest more than the recommended dose"), on product warning labels ("Harmful if ingested"), in toxicology reports ("If ingested, seek immediate medical attention"), and in biology textbooks ("The organism ingests nutrients from the surrounding environment").
The Technical Meaning in Computers and Data

In technology and data science, "ingest" has taken on a second, extended meaning. When a computer system ingests data, it means the system is taking in large amounts of data from an external source in order to store, process, or analyze it. For example: "The pipeline ingests thousands of records per second," or "The AI model ingests training data before it can learn." This is a direct metaphor borrowed from the biological meaning — just as a body takes in food and processes it into energy and nutrients, a computer system takes in raw data and processes it into something useful.

The noun form of "ingest" is ingestion, referring to the act or process of ingesting. "Ingestion of alcohol on an empty stomach can be dangerous." "The ingestion of the medication should be followed by a full glass of water." This form appears constantly in medical, scientific, and legal writing, so it is just as worth knowing as the verb itself.

To ingest means to take a substance into the body — typically by swallowing — so the body can process it. In technology, it means to take data into a system for processing. It is a formal, precise word that works for food, medicine, poison, foreign objects, and even data, making it far more versatile than everyday words like "eat" or "drink."
